title: Outage: three office PCs drop off the network on and off

lines.text: 08:30 office manager: the front desk PC and two others say 'No internet' on and off since Monday; the rest are fine. Client uploads close at 09:30.
RTR-OFFICE rebooting: every PC and the phones are offline for about 5 minutes
RTR-OFFICE restored to factory defaults: port forwarding, the printer reservation and the Wi-Fi settings are gone
09:30 the client upload portal closed; the front desk batch was not sent

brief.situation: You are the on-call technician for Birchwood Bookkeeping, a fictional nine-person office. Since Monday the front desk PC and two others lose the internet and the file share on and off; the other six PCs are fine. The front desk must upload today's client batch before the portal closes at 09:30. It is 08:30.
handover: RTR-OFFICE (192.168.1.1) is the router, firewall and only DHCP server: it hands out 192.168.1.100-199. The file share is on 192.168.1.10. An unmanaged switch feeds the desks and the conference room.
RTR-OFFICE forwards a port for the remote bookkeeper's VPN and holds a reservation for the printer. A consultant has been working in the conference room this week.
howItWorks: Run commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's commands run; there is no free shell, and each command's arguments come from its list.
Each command takes your time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The deadline keeps coming on the same clock.
The map shows the router, the switch, the PCs and anything you find, each with a status in words. Output appears in the terminal as it happens.
When you declare the problem fixed, you write the ticket and explain your reasoning.

source.note: How many minutes each command or task takes, and when the fictional problem spreads, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. The upload portal closes at 09:30, 60 minutes after the first report.

The internet provider's line was dropping

writeup.question: For the ticket: what told you this was not the internet line or the PCs, where the wrong addresses came from and how you proved it, and why your fix covers every PC.

parts.label: Symptom
parts.criteria: Reads the affected PCs' 192.168.8.x address, gateway and DHCP server against a working PC's 192.168.1.x from 192.168.1.1, and says six PCs working rules out the internet line.
parts.modelAnswer: ipconfig /all on FRONT-PC showed 192.168.8.23 with gateway, DNS and DHCP server 192.168.8.1; a working PC had 192.168.1.42 from 192.168.1.1. Six PCs worked, so the line and the router were fine; the three PCs were on the wrong network.

parts.label: Source and proof
parts.criteria: Identifies a second DHCP server answering on the LAN (the travel router), confirmed by RTR-OFFICE's client list lacking the three PCs and by finding the device.
parts.modelAnswer: RTR-OFFICE's DHCP list did not have the three PCs, so another server was answering. A client takes one of the offers it gets, often the first, so some PCs got the wrong one. The consultant's travel router was plugged into the conference room jack by its LAN port.

parts.label: Fix that covers everyone
parts.criteria: Removes the second server at its source (not a static address on one PC or a router reset), then renews every affected PC and checks it.
parts.modelAnswer: I unplugged the travel router, then released and renewed the three PCs; each got a 192.168.1.x lease and reached the share. A static address would have fixed one PC and left the server answering, and a factory reset would have wiped the VPN forward and the printer reservation without touching the cause.

source.cite: Infrastructure outcome profile (docs/sims.md 9.2, 22.10), tightened to 30 minutes for this case
source.note: Fixed with time to spare before the 09:30 upload deadline; the scenario's own timing.
No second fault: an office-wide router reboot or a factory reset.

noProgress.rationale: Closing with the second DHCP server still answering leaves PCs on a network with no internet whenever they renew; it is never a safe outcome.

expertPath.text: ipconfig /all on FRONT-PC and on a working PC: 192.168.8.23 from DHCP server 192.168.8.1 against 192.168.1.42 from 192.168.1.1.
RTR-OFFICE's DHCP list lacks the three PCs; trace the switch ports and find the travel router in the conference room jack.
Unplug it, then release and renew FRONT-PC and the other two; each gets 192.168.1.x and reaches the share.
Ticket: second DHCP server; ask visitors to use guest Wi-Fi, and consider a switch that supports DHCP snooping.

fixed.headline: Good: fixed at the source
fixed.body: You compared the DHCP server in a bad lease with a good one, found the second server and removed it, then renewed every PC it had reached.

fixedGaps.headline: Fixed, with gaps
fixedGaps.body: The office works. The criteria show what it cost: time, a change before the evidence, a PC left on a typed-in address, a PC not renewed or a reboot.

routerWiped.headline: The reset made it worse
routerWiped.body: The router was not the problem: its DHCP list simply lacked the three PCs. A factory reset wiped the VPN forward and the printer reservation and left the travel router answering.

deadlineMissed.headline: The deadline passed
deadlineMissed.body: ipconfig /all on the front desk PC named the wrong DHCP server in the first two minutes. Driver reinstalls and waiting did not touch it.

stillDown.headline: Closed too soon
stillDown.body: A static address fixed one PC. The second DHCP server kept answering, so the other two stayed down and any PC that renews can join them.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No ticket was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Three PCs failing on and off while six work points away from the internet line. ipconfig /all on an affected PC shows 192.168.8.23 with gateway, DNS and DHCP server 192.168.8.1, against a working PC's 192.168.1.42 from 192.168.1.1, so a second DHCP server is answering; a client takes one of the offers it gets, often the first. RTR-OFFICE's DHCP list lacks the three PCs, and tracing the switch finds a travel router plugged into the conference room jack by its LAN port. Unplug it, then release and renew each affected PC and check it reaches the share. A static address fixes one PC only, and a factory reset wipes the router's settings without touching the cause.
